extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning how to write proofs (first-year university)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for writing clear, correct, and conventional mathematical proofs and definitions at the introductory undergraduate level (sets, logic, notation, exposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate mathematics, not just compute
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is not simply number crunching or using formulas — this is using mathematics. Mathematics is also about understanding and reasoning and most importantly proving things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise both doing mathematics and explaining it; proofs exist to explain why something is true — treat the proof as a dialog between you and the reader. Think of the reader when writing: be clear, precise and accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, precision, and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Make every (reasonable) effort to be clear, precise and accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care of your reader and use clear language and enough detail so they can follow along. Avoid obfuscation and personal shorthand unless fully explained; use standard notation to avoid confusing the reader (example: do not use ε in place of ∈).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the reader (three reader-types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about three different readers: you (the writer), another person (e.g., marker), and an imaginary pedantic reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the level of explanation and notation so that someone not present (e.g., the person marking your exam) can follow the written argument. Use the imaginary pedant to check clarity: would they ask 'Is that the right notation?' or 'Does the logic flow?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs are structured logical dialogs
rubrics_metrics.description: The sentences in a proof are arranged in a particular order and cannot be shuffled; each one implies the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use connective words and phrases (e.g., 'hence', 'this tells us', 'because of this') to emphasise logical connections. Ensure the logical flow is explicit and that each step justifies the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do rough work, then write a neat proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Behind every proof you read (and you write) lies a good bit of rough work; map out structure and details first then write the proof nicely and neatly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest time in drafting: first work out the structure and computations, then produce a clear final write-up. Presenting work well helps both writer and reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms and conventions explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: You must define key terms and conventions because readers may have different backgrounds (e.g., whether 0 is a natural number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give precise definitions when needed (example given: even integer = two times another integer). State your convention choices (e.g., whether 0 is included in N) to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and explain standard notation (consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many conventions in mathematics; using standard ones makes it easier for readers to understand your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use capital letters for sets (A, B, C), lower case letters for elements (a, b, c), use blackboard bold for standard sets (N, Z, Q, R). Pick a notation for operations like negation (~, ¬, or !) and stick with it throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific symbol conventions: membership and sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ∈ for 'is an element of' and ∉ for 'is not an element of'; use braces {·} for sets (not parentheses/brackets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute nonstandard symbols (example: stop using ε for ∈). Use braces to list set elements; order and repetition do not matter in a set listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter usage conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose variable letters according to standard mathematical practice to aid readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: i,j,k,l,m,n usually denote integers; x,y,z,w usually denote real numbers. Avoid unusual choices that confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set description must answer 'is this object in the set?'
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining a set ensure the definition lets the reader decide membership unambiguously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good example: 'Let A be the set of even integers between 1 and 13.' Bad example: 'Let B be the set of tall people in this classroom.' For small finite sets list elements; for larger/infinite sets use set-builder notation with a precise rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate notation for larger or infinite sets (set-builder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use set-builder notation for sets too large to list, e.g. S = { x | x is even and positive }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the vertical bar '|' or ':' to mean 'such that'. Ensure the expression or rule is precise; avoid ambiguous ellipses unless the pattern is completely clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of ellipsis and patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The ellipsis '...' is shorthand for missing entries and instructs to follow a pattern, but can be ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use '...' when the pattern is unambiguous from context; add extra words when necessary (examples of ambiguous sets like {3,5,7,...} need clarification whether they mean odd primes or all odd numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-referential and paradoxical constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-referential definitions (e.g., Russell's set S = {A | A ∉ A}) lead to paradox and should be avoided at this level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of definitions that refer to the object being defined; avoid sentences like 'This sentence is false.' If such topics arise, handle them only with appropriate formal foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open sentences require domain specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions with free variables (open sentences) are not statements until a domain/value is specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing P(x) indicate the domain for x (integers, reals, etc.) so the truth value becomes well-defined; for multiple variables use P(x,k) etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for commonly-known sets and symbols should be standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Use blackboard-bold letters for N, Z, Q, R; avoid nonstandard notation that can be confused with other symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between regular boldface and blackboard bold (N ≠ N, R ≠ R). Clarify any nonstandard choices you make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about singleton vs set-of-empty-set distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and write distinctions like ∅ vs {∅} vs {{∅}} carefully, since they are common sources of confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give examples to illustrate differences; ensure proofs and set manipulations respect these distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and stick to a negation notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation can be written as ∼P, !P or ¬P; the text uses the tilde but recognises the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent in your choice of notation to avoid confusing the reader; recognise alternative notations so you can read others' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous variable naming in set-builder and expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorrect or inconsistent use of bound variables causes ambiguity (exercise examples demonstrate many wrong forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing sets like {2n+1 : n ∈ N} ensure the bound variable appears consistently and is not reused or mismatched; document common anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient detail but expect reasonable reader competence
rubrics_metrics.description: You should provide enough explanation that a reader who knows standard notation and basic algebra can follow, but need not spell out extremely trivial arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike balance: don't omit steps that hide logical connections; don't be overly verbose where standard inference suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for decimal/base representations and uniqueness rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When using decimal expansions, choose canonical representations (avoid representations ending in all nines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the chosen convention for representations (example: prefer expansions ending in zeros rather than repeating nines) to maintain injectivity in constructions involving digits.

rubrics_metrics.name: When constructing functions or bijections, handle edge cases explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: In proofs constructing maps (e.g., g((a,b)) = 0.a1b1a2b2...), check injectivity/surjectivity carefully, and address non-uniqueness of representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit choices (e.g., forbidding decimal expansions that end in infinite nines) and justify why that removes ambiguity; show how special examples are or are not in the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with informal historical/ philosophical tangents
rubrics_metrics.description: The text sometimes refers readers to external searches or background (history of zero, Russell’s paradox) but these are supplementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep such digressions clearly marked as optional background and do not let them substitute for precise definitions required in proofs.
